headings.title: Introduction to Anatomical Terminology
headings.content: Anatomy relies on a precise language to describe the human body clearly without ambiguity. Medical professionals across Nigeria and the world use a shared set of terms derived mostly from Latin and Greek roots. This vocabulary prevents confusion when charting patient notes, giving handovers, or discussing surgical sites. Breaking down terms into prefixes, roots, and suffixes makes memorization much easier. For instance, knowing that "peri-" means around and "cardio" means heart immediately tells you the pericardium is the sac surrounding the heart.

headings.title: The Standard Anatomical Position
headings.content:
- **Posture**: The body stands upright in an erect posture.
- **Limbs**: Upper limbs hang straight down by the sides.
- **Head and Gaze**: The face looks forward straight ahead, with eyes open.
- **Palms**: The palms of the hands face forward, with thumbs pointing away from the body.
- **Feet**: Lower limbs are parallel, with toes pointing directly forward.

Failing to picture this position leads to incorrect charting of wounds, rashes, or surgical incisions.

headings.title: Anatomical Planes of the Body
headings.content:
Imaginary flat surfaces called anatomical planes slice through the body to help visualize internal structures and injuries. 

1. **Sagittal Plane**: Runs vertically, dividing the body into right and left portions. When it cuts directly down the exact midline, it is called the midsagittal or median plane.
2. **Frontal Plane**: Also known as the coronal plane, this vertical cut divides the body into anterior and posterior parts.
3. **Transverse Plane**: Runs horizontally, cutting the body at a right angle to the vertical axes to create superior and inferior sections.

headings.title: Directional Terms and Their Clinical Application
headings.content:
Directional terms describe the location of one body structure relative to another. 

| Term | Definition | Example |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Anterior (Ventral)** | Toward the front of the body | The sternum is anterior to the heart |
| **Posterior (Dorsal)** | Toward the back of the body | The spine is posterior to the trachea |
| **Superior (Cranial)** | Toward the head or upper part | The head is superior to the abdomen |
| **Inferior (Caudal)** | Away from the head or lower part | The pelvis is inferior to the ribs |
| **Medial** | Toward the midline of the body | The big toe is on the medial side of the foot |
| **Lateral** | Away from the midline of the body | The arms are lateral to the chest |
| **Proximal** | Closer to the point of attachment | The elbow is proximal to the wrist |
| **Distal** | Farther from the point of attachment | The fingers are distal to the elbow |

Misusing proximal and distal during a wound dressing change can lead to charting errors in the patient's record.

headings.title: Body Cavities and Major Organs
headings.content:
The body contains internal spaces called cavities that protect, separate, and support delicate organs. The two main divisions are the dorsal and ventral cavities.

The dorsal cavity protects the nervous system and contains the cranial cavity for the brain and the spinal cavity for the spinal cord. 

The larger ventral cavity houses visceral organs in the chest and abdomen. It splits into the thoracic cavity, enclosed by the ribcage, and the abdominopelvic cavity below it. A dome-shaped muscle called the diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity.

headings.title: Abdominopelvic Regions and Quadrants
headings.content:
To accurately document pain, tenderness, or masses, healthcare providers divide the large abdominopelvic area into smaller sections. 

Dividing the area with two vertical and two horizontal lines creates four quadrants: the **right upper quadrant**, **left upper quadrant**, **right lower quadrant**, and **left lower quadrant**. 

For more specific anatomical mapping, clinicians use a nine-region grid created by two vertical and two horizontal tic-tac-toe lines. These regions include the **hypochondriac**, **lumbar**, and **iliac** regions on the sides, with the **epigastric**, **umbilical**, and **hypogastric** regions running down the middle.
